title: Fed Pivots to Tightening and the Long End Keeps Selling Off
content:
The window's dominant story was a Fed that confirmed its turn back to tightening. On 16 September the FOMC raised its target range by 25bp to **3.75%-4.00%**, its first hike since 2023, with a dot plot flagging one further move this year as core PCE was pencilled near **3.4%**.

The sharper action came at the long end. The US 10-year pushed to roughly **5.32%**, its highest since 2002, and the 30-year reached about **5.70%**, while short rates slipped — a textbook **bear-steepening** driven by sticky inflation, heavy issuance and term-premium repricing. Odds of an October follow-up faded from near half to under a fifth, even as a December hike stayed live.

Higher long yields lifted discount rates across equities, credit and housing and underpinned the dollar. With the curve doing much of the Fed's work, auction demand and incoming inflation prints became the key swing factors into year-end.

title: Equities Grind to Records Even as Discount Rates Climb
content:
The equity market's defiance of surging yields became a theme in itself. The S&P 500 kept carving fresh highs, posting its first close above **7,800** on 9 October, even as the 10-year marched towards 5.3% — a backdrop that would normally pressure the richest valuations.

Leadership stayed narrow, tethered to a handful of AI megacaps whose capex plans and earnings optimism offset the drag from higher rates. The resulting **narrow breadth** left benchmarks hostage to a few names, and bouts of selling arrived whenever yields or oil spiked, as during 6-8 October when the index slipped back from its record.

The set-up sharpened the central question into Q4: whether AI-driven earnings can keep justifying stretched multiples as discount rates rise. With megacaps steering direction, their durability remained the market's principal vulnerability.

title: Gold Consolidates in Record Territory as a Debasement Hedge
content:
Gold's entrenchment near record highs stayed a defining cross-asset signal. Bullion held well above **$4,000** throughout, having earlier touched the **$4,400s** before easing back towards **$4,200** by the second week of October — a consolidation rather than a reversal.

The resilience was notable because it persisted against a firm dollar and multi-decade-high real yields, usually stiff headwinds for a non-yielding asset. Steady central-bank buying and robust investor demand instead pointed to a structural **debasement hedge** against large deficits, sticky inflation and geopolitical risk.

With both long bonds and the priciest equities wobbling, gold offered diversification few assets could match. Its ability to hold firm despite high real rates made its momentum a closely watched gauge of underlying investor anxiety into year-end.

title: Middle East Supply Risk Keeps a Premium Embedded in Crude
content:
A persistent Middle East **supply shock** ran through the window, with constrained flows around the Strait of Hormuz and fresh attacks on Gulf energy infrastructure keeping a risk premium in crude even as regional output slowly recovered.

Prices stayed elevated but two-way. Brent had spiked above **$109** earlier in the period before settling near **$104**, with WTI around **$92**, as alternative export routes and gradually rising capacity capped the upside against recurring supply scares.

The shock mattered because energy fed directly into hotter inflation prints and hawkish central-bank rhetoric, reinforcing the higher-for-longer narrative that drove the bond rout. A renewed Hormuz disruption remained the key upside tail for prices — and the main downside tail for global risk assets.
